title: Protein’s Many Jobs Explain Why “More” Is a Complicated Claim
summary:
A protein label can appear on pancake mix, popcorn or even a drink. But does a bigger number on the package mean a better food? Smithsonian asked nutrition experts, and their answer depends on health, goals and the food supplying the protein.

Protein is a macronutrient, one of the nutrients the body needs in relatively large amounts. Carbohydrates and fats are others. The body breaks dietary protein into amino acids, then rearranges those building blocks into new proteins. Humans use 20 types of amino acids; nine are essential, meaning they must come from food.

Nutrition researcher Teresa Fung explains that proteins do much more than make muscle. They are found in organs and many hormones. Infection-fighting antibodies are proteins, as are enzymes involved in digestion and other processes.

Adult guidance has changed. An older widely used benchmark was about 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight daily. The World Health Organization's recommendation is close to that, at 0.83 grams. The Smithsonian report says U.S. federal guidance updated in January 2026 suggests 1.2 to 1.6 grams per kilogram. These adult figures are not presented as targets for children.

Some experts welcome the new range. David Allison says he would have made a similar decision. Exercise physiologist Stuart Phillips agrees, while emphasizing physical activity. He says even athletes training intensively usually stop seeing large benefits beyond 1.6 grams per kilogram, though bodybuilders may differ.

Dietician Daphene Altema-Johnson says most Americans already eat within the updated range. Adding protein does not automatically make a cookie or pastry healthier. A person's goals or health circumstances may change their needs, but a package label alone cannot answer that question.

Fung also explains that the body cannot simply stash unused protein in a store. Unused amino acids can become energy. People with certain kidney, liver or amino-acid-processing conditions work with health professionals on their diets.

The story is therefore about context, not chasing the largest protein number. The nutrient is important, and so are the rest of the food, a person's activity and individual health needs.
why_it_matters: Protein has many jobs in the body. Understanding those jobs and the food around it helps explain why a protein label does not describe a food’s whole nutritional value.
